newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to ditch five-day bank opening limit.
newsitem.headline: France to ditch five-day bank opening limit.

text.p: The French government will revise a 60-year-old decree to allow banks to open six days a week instead of five, labour minister Jacques Barrot said on Tuesday.

Barrot told a news conference banks and unions had failed to reach agreement and that the government would therefore go ahead with proposals to repeal the 1937 banking hours decree to allow bank branches to stay open from Monday to Saturday.
Unions called a one-day strike on Friday on the grounds that the government was preparing to change banking hours regulation without sufficient negotiation.
Barrot said he would propose a new decree to the cabinet meeting on Wednesday and that it would also allow banks to open from 0730 to 2030 each day, ending the current eight-hour limit.
"The 1937 decree belongs to an era, that of 1937," he said. "People need to be able to go to the bank on Saturday".

Barrot said the original proposals for the 1997 decree had been modified after consultation and that they now contained an obligation on banks to convene a works council meeting if changes in opening hours had not won employee approval.
Sunday would remain a "rest day" for all banks and staff would still be guaranteed a two-day break each week, he said.

Barrot said that the French commercial banking association (AFB) had agreed that the new decree would be put in to practice gradually and that the association believed the greater flexibility could preserve about 9,000 jobs that would otherwise have been at risk.
Some French banks have been able to open on Saturday because of their special status but the aim is to generalise this to commercial banks which have been unable to do so.
